TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Intervenor Jason A. Howton files this response under SOAH Order No. 35 to Applicants' Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (Applicants' Brief) and Commission Staff's Initial Brief on Remand (Staff Brief). It answers only what those briefs say. It incorporates Intervenor's October 7 brief by reference and does not repeat it. Factual statements below cite admitted exhibits, the certified hearing transcript, and the Proposal for Decision (PFD). Pleadings, and orders in other dockets, are cited for what they are: a party's position, or the Commission's decision on its own record.
I.	SUMMARY OF RESPONSE
The Commission remanded for answers drawn from record data. The Chairman called the two issues "critical and crucial to the decision we're going to make," and Commissioner Jackson stated that the ALJs "need to provide the data and information that's necessary for us to make the decision." On this record, the data answer both questions against Applicants.
Applicants' own filings answer Issue No. 11. In this docket they state that ERCOT "performs RTP studies annually to demonstrate compliance with NERC standards," and that "[s]pecial ERCOT studies like the PBRP are not required to, and generally are not intended to, independently demonstrate compliance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1." Their October 7 brief then states that the 2024 and 2025 RTPs "assume the Import Path 2 Projects are in service, and the record contains no power-flow study or other technical analysis modeling a reliable alternative with those facilities removed."
Those statements close a circle. The study that created Import Path 2 was not intended to demonstrate compliance with TPL-001-5.1. The studies that are intended to demonstrate compliance began with Import Path 2 already in service. No study in the record asks whether the system meets the standard without it. A finding that these facilities are "necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards" would rest on an assumption that was never tested.
Applicants' own numbers answer Issue No. 13. The $229 million in annual consumer savings they cite is ERCOT's long-term comparison of two statewide plans. The same ERCOT table shows that in study year 2034 the 765-kV plan costs consumers $136 million more than the 345-kV plan. Staff reproduces those figures and concedes that "the 345-kV Plan provides more savings than the 765-kV Plan for the 2034 study year." None of those dollars is attributed to these facilities.
Finally, the answer to Issue No. 11 decides which need test applies. It does not decide whether need was shown. The ALJs' findings that need was not established stand however Issue No. 11 is answered.
II.	ISSUE NO. 11: APPLICANTS AND STAFF DO NOT IDENTIFY A RELIABILITY STANDARD THAT REQUIRES THESE FACILITIES
A.	Applicants' own filings close the circle.
Applicants lead with ERCOT's statement that the PBRP reliability assessments "were performed based on NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1." Intervenor does not dispute that ERCOT used the standard's contingency categories when it built the PBRP. The narrower point is what Applicants say that use means. Seven days before their brief, they told the Commission that special studies like the PBRP "are not required to, and generally are not intended to, independently demonstrate compliance" with TPL-001-5.1, and that the annual RTPs serve that purpose. Their brief then concedes that the RTPs "assume the Import Path 2 Projects are in service."
Applicants cannot rely on the PBRP as proof of TPL-001-5.1 compliance after disclaiming that role for it. Nor can they rely on the RTPs as proof of necessity when the RTPs began with the line in the model. A test that starts with the bridge already built cannot show whether the river needs one.
B.	The federal statute Applicants cite says reliability standards do not require new transmission.
Applicants are right that federal law makes NERC reliability standards mandatory and that ERCOT must plan to them. For that proposition they cite 16 U.S.C. § 824o(a)(3). That subsection defines "reliability standard," and it also states that "the term does not include any requirement to enlarge such facilities or to construct new transmission capacity or generation capacity." When a planning assessment finds a deficiency, TPL-001-5.1 requires a corrective action plan, and that plan may take several forms. The source Applicants cite does not support their conclusion that the standard requires these facilities.
C.	The violations ERCOT reported do not identify one that these facilities cure.
Applicants describe thermal overloads, voltage instability, and unsolved power flows in ERCOT's 2030 and 2038 PBRP study cases. Intervenor accepts that ERCOT reported those results. Three record facts limit what they prove about these facilities.
First, for 2030, "ERCOT considered only a 345-kV import path option." Second, for 2038, ERCOT's own comparison reports that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import path options each "[m]eets ERCOT and NERC Reliability Criteria." That comparison shows that the reliability criteria did not uniquely require the 765-kV configuration for which Applicants now seek certification. Third, both study cases were built on load the ALJs found overstated, with a non-oil-and-gas reduction of at least 3,571 MW. The ALJs have already found that NERC contingencies "are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for Import Path 2." Applicants' brief does not engage that finding.
The same is true of the N-0 voltage instability Applicants cite in the Delaware Basin. It appears in the 2038 case, and Applicants cite no study tying it to these facilities rather than to the other PBRP facilities.
D.	An operating limit under FAC-011-4 is not a violation that these facilities cure.
Applicants now describe the Far West Import GTCs as "a second and independent NERC violation," and state that "failure to build Import Path 2 eliminates the solution." Intervenor does not minimize an interconnection reliability operating limit. Exceeding one can cause serious harm, which is why FAC-011-4 governs how such limits are established. That is the narrower point. FAC-011-4 sets a methodology for establishing operating limits, and an established limit is how the system is kept within reliable bounds. Designating a limit is not a finding that a standard has been violated, and FAC-011-4 does not direct what facilities are built.
The record also does not support "eliminates the solution." The GTCs "have not resulted in any load shed to date." ERCOT listed the 765-kV import paths as one of seven upgrades that would "help" exit the constraints. Applicants' witness did not run the power flows behind that list. The exit strategy addressed a case in which about 2,500 MW of planned Permian dispatchable generation materializes, while the ALJs found 25.162 GW of Permian gas projects under construction, in pre-construction, or announced. The ALJs found that the GTCs "do not validate the PBRP's original load forecast or the necessity for Import Path 2."
E.	Great weight cannot be moved from the PBRP to studies that assumed the line.
Applicants argue that the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP, and the April 2026 exit strategy are each "entitled independently to 'great weight.'" The rule does give great weight to an ERCOT recommendation, and Intervenor does not ask the ALJs to set it aside. The rule attaches that weight on a condition: the recommendation must be "substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth." The ALJs found the PBRP recommendation did not meet it.
The new theory fails for three reasons. First, the RTPs did not independently establish Import Path 2's necessity by comparing the system with and without it; they started with it in service, as Applicants now concede. An assumption in a start case is not a recommendation that a facility is necessary. Second, the PBRP load forecast "has not been subjected to or retested against ERCOT's adjusted methodology," and no ERCOT study retested these facilities at the adjusted load. Third, the ALJs found that "[e]ven affording great weight to ERCOT's PBRP 765-kV recommendation, the greater weight of the credible evidence is against the recommendation." Great weight does not make ERCOT's recommendation determinative of the Commission's ultimate need finding.
The Directory points to ERCOT's reduced-load sensitivity, in which key needs "remained similar." That sensitivity priced both plans "under the sensitivity case including the Permian Basin Reliability Import Path," used 2026, 2027, and 2029 cases, and did not isolate these facilities. Applicants also stated in discovery that they had "not performed an analysis to determine whether a 20 percent reduction in projected load growth would affect the need for 765 kV infrastructure specifically." Applicants themselves describe the test as "whether the recommended facilities remain needed across credible dispatch and load sensitivities." No study in the record runs these facilities through the adjusted load the ALJs found.
The Commission's own rules now say what large-load forecast is substantiated enough for transmission planning. Section 25.370, adopted in February 2026, sets "criteria for including the load of a large load customer in ERCOT's load forecasts used for identifying transmission planning needs." Under subsection (c), that demand is not included "unless the large load customer executed an interconnection agreement as required under §25.194 of this Title and provided all of the disclosures and financial commitments required for such an agreement under §25.194 of this Title." Section 25.194, which the PFD described as proposed, took effect October 8, 2026. Intervenor does not argue that either rule applies retroactively to the PBRP. The point is narrower. Fifty-five percent of the PBRP's non-oil-and-gas load rested on an officer letter, and 6 percent was unconfirmed. Load of that kind would not ordinarily qualify for inclusion in a transmission-planning forecast under the Commission's current criteria. That is consistent with the ALJs' finding that the PBRP recommendation was not substantiated.
F.	The Import Path 1 and Import Path 3 orders do not answer Issue No. 11 on this record.
Applicants ask the ALJs to adopt findings from the Commission's orders approving Import Paths 1 and 3, and argue there is "no valid reason to reach a different conclusion for Import Path 2." The ALJs may consider those orders as Commission decisions, and Intervenor does not suggest otherwise. But findings of fact "may be based only on the evidence and on matters that are officially noticed." Applicants have not shown that those other-docket findings are evidence in this docket or matters officially noticed.
Those orders also do not decide the question remanded here. The Docket No. 59336 order, for example, finds that "[t]he applicants demonstrated a reasonable need for the proposed transmission facilities." Its need findings do not find that Import Path 3 is necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard. Applicants' proposed findings, drawn from those orders, also state that "the applicants did not independently evaluate alternatives." The ALJs made the same finding here.
This record holds evidence that bears on Import Path 2 specifically. ERCOT's December 12, 2024 Sequencing Letter states that "two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030." The Commission has now certificated two. The ALJs weighed that letter, the adjusted load, the post-PBRP generation, and the absence of a partial-build study. Intervenor asks that the supplemental PFD state that the ALJs considered the Import Path 1 and 3 orders, that those orders found reasonable need on their own records, and that the findings here rest on the evidence in this docket. Findings stated that way give the Commission the record basis it must address before changing a finding of the ALJs.
Nor are those orders final. A contested-case order becomes final when the latest timely motion for rehearing is overruled. Motions for rehearing challenging the need findings are pending against the Import Path 3 order. In Docket No. 59029, the Commission extended its time to act on the Import Path 1 motions "to the maximum extent allowed by law," after the Chairman recommended the extension to "allow the Commission to fully consider all the arguments raised in these motions." Applicants ask the ALJs to adopt findings that remain subject to pending motions for rehearing.
G.	An "untested variable" is a concession, and the burden is Applicants'.
Applicants say that "no independent analysis or planning study shows that the plan would still resolve the identified reliability issues without" Import Path 2, and that removing it "would introduce an untested variable." The Commission grants a certificate "only if it finds that the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public." Applicants carry that burden by a preponderance of the evidence. A study that has never been run is a gap in Applicants' proof. Calling the facility's absence "untested" concedes that its necessity was never tested either.
The record does contain a tested alternative. ERCOT's 2024 RTP 345-kV plan identified 274 reliability projects "to address all reliability violations." And the one witness asked about a partial-build study said he "assume[d]" the multi-line recommendation followed from TPL-001's contingency requirements. Removing an element during a contingency study is not the same as studying the system without that element.
H.	The voltage comparisons chose among options; they did not test need.
Applicants' proposed findings describe the Commission's voltage decision as an evaluation of "the carrying capacity, estimated costs, engineering, procurement, and construction of the 765-kV alternative" against the 345-kV and 500-kV options. They state that no alternative would "more efficiently resolve all the reliability issues." That is a comparison, and a legitimate one. Staff's witness agreed that Staff's voltage analysis was limited to "issues unique to each voltage" and set aside "market-wide common risk factors like import tariffs." The STEP comparison in JG-4 is the same kind of document: its starting cases carried the three import paths, and its results are differences between two plans. Comparing two trucks on price and payload shows which truck to buy. It does not show that a truck is needed. Issue No. 11 asks the latter question.
I.	An export benefit is an economic benefit.
Applicants argue that the facilities will operate bidirectionally and reduce "the need to curtail Permian Basin exports of cost-effective generation." Intervenor agrees that a transmission line can carry power in either direction. The PBRP's stated purpose for Import Path 2, as the ALJs found, was to bring power into the Permian Basin. Applicants' witness describes the export function in price terms: Permian thermal units "could not compete with local wind and solar resources on price." That is an economic benefit of the facility. It may bear on Issue No. 13, but it does not itself identify a reliability standard that requires these facilities. An export function also makes the source-end findings more important, not less.
J.	Whatever the answer to Issue No. 11, the need findings stand.
Applicants say that a project required to cure NERC violations is, "by definition, needed to provide reliable service." Staff makes the same move in fewer words. The rule does not work that way. A line necessary to meet reliability standards is exempt from the economic tests in clause (i). Its need is then evaluated under subclause (II), which applies "[f]or a transmission line not addressed by clause (i)" and directs the Commission to consider load and the needs of the interconnected system. The ALJs applied that subclause and found need not established.
The answer to Issue No. 11 therefore selects the test. It does not pass it. Intervenor asks the ALJs to say so in a conclusion of law (proposed RCL-4 below), so that the Commission reads any answer to Issue No. 11 together with the findings that decide need.
III.	ISSUE NO. 13: THE FIGURES APPLICANTS AND STAFF CITE DO NOT ESTIMATE SAVINGS FROM THESE FACILITIES
A.	The $229 million is ERCOT's long-term figure; the 2034 figure runs the other way.
Applicants say the 765-kV plan "will deliver approximately $229 million in additional annual consumer energy cost savings." ERCOT labels that figure "Long-term." ERCOT's consumer energy cost results, as Staff reproduces them, are:

The $229 million is the 2039 difference between the two plans. In 2034, the 765-kV plan costs consumers $136 million more than the 345-kV plan. Measured against the base case, the 765-kV plan saves $63 million in 2034 and $156 million in 2039. Staff agrees that "the 345-kV Plan provides more savings than the 765-kV Plan for the 2034 study year." ERCOT also estimates the 765-kV plan's construction cost at $2.24 billion more than the 345-kV plan's.
B.	A comparison of two statewide plans is not an estimate of savings "from the proposed transmission facilities."
Every forward-looking figure Applicants cite is stated "compared to expanding the existing 345 kV network." Issue No. 13 asks what savings "may result from the proposed transmission facilities." The congestion test asks whether "the levelized ERCOT-wide annual congestion cost savings attributable to the proposed project" meet a threshold set by the project's first-year annual revenue requirement. No figure in either brief assigns any amount to these facilities, and the record contains no first-year revenue requirement for them. A fence post cannot be measured by the length of the whole fence.
The historical figures carry the same limit. The Independent Market Monitor's estimate of ERCOT-wide congestion costs from 2020 through 2024 describes a problem. It does not estimate how much of that problem these facilities would relieve. Oncor told its investors and the Securities and Exchange Commission that "there is no guarantee that the execution of STEP and the PBRP will eliminate or reduce the amount of congestion within the ERCOT system."
C.	The cost half of the PURA § 37.056(d) comparison is also missing.
For a line not necessary to meet reliability standards, the Commission's criteria must include "a comparison of the estimated cost of the transmission project for consumers and the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers." The PFD found that Applicants supplied construction cost, not cost to consumers, and that tariff exposure was not analyzed. The record shows why that gap matters. Applicants' route cost estimates are dated March 26, 2026. Applicants' cost witness agreed that the estimates for all 122 routes "contained no line item [for] Section 232 tariff exposure on structural steel or aluminum, including tariffs put in place by the President on April 2nd, 2026," and that the pricing "assumes imported steel structures and imported large-power transformers." The April 2, 2026 proclamation, effective April 6, applies a 50 percent duty to the full customs value of covered steel and aluminum articles "regardless of metal content," and its annex lists steel lattice towers and steel-cored aluminum conductor. Staff set the same exposure aside, and its witness agreed there is "no line item for tariffs."
Intervenor does not suggest that the duty raises total project cost by 50 percent. It reaches imported covered articles, not right-of-way, labor, or domestic material. The point is narrower. The estimates price the structures as imports and carry no duty on them, and the record contains no bill of materials or sourcing data to measure the effect. ERCOT's planning figures share the limit. The PBRP priced the 345-kV option from transmission service providers' estimates and states that the "MISO 2024 Transmission Cost Estimation Guide was referenced for the EHV options (500-kV or 765-kV)." Both sets of figures date from 2024, before the April 2026 proclamation, and the 765-kV figure comes from a general industry guide rather than from estimates prepared for these facilities. The congestion test sets savings levelized over the long term against a first-year revenue requirement. With a pre-tariff planning estimate on the cost side, that comparison cannot be made on this record. The point applies to either voltage. It bears on the comparison PURA requires, not on the choice between plans.
D.	No witness measured the savings.
Applicants' reliability witness offered no opinion on the cost of Import Path 2 and did not compare it to any alternative. Staff's witness agreed that he had done "no independent analysis or review on the costs regarding the import path" and relied on Applicants' cost testimony. On this record, the answer to Issue No. 13 is that the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from these facilities have not been established.
IV.	RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF
Staff answers Issue No. 11 "Yes." Intervenor respects Staff's role in this proceeding. Four points limit the weight its answer can carry.
First, Staff's answer rests on argument. Its first two footnotes quote Applicants' exceptions to the PFD, and its discussion of the RTPs and exit strategies cites Applicants' Directory "generally." SOAH Order No. 35 requires "specific pinpoint citations from the record." The only evidence Staff cites is its witness's direct testimony restating the PBRP.
Second, Staff's witness supplied the qualifications. He agreed that the basis for need "is from the Commission-approved Permian Basin Reliability Plan" and that he had not done "any independent study regarding the need for the import paths at issue in this docket." He agreed that, given changed conditions, re-evaluation of the forecasted demand is warranted. And asked to assume negative natural-gas prices at the Waha hub, he agreed it could "potentially" be more cost effective overall to ratepayers for LCRA or another legislatively created entity to own and operate dispatchable gas generation in the Path 2 area than to build Import Path 2.
Third, Staff does not engage the findings that decide need: the absence of a partial-build study, the 2030 finding, the adjusted load, or the finding that the evidence outweighs ERCOT's recommendation even with great weight. An answer to Issue No. 11 that does not address those findings does not change them.
Fourth, Staff's alternative answer on Issue No. 13 supports Intervenor. Staff's own figures show the 345-kV plan saving consumers $199 million against the base case in 2034, compared with $63 million for the 765-kV plan. Staff also relies on lower congestion rent. Congestion rent is not the consumer congestion cost savings that Issue No. 13 and PURA § 37.056(d) ask about, and none of Staff's figures is attributed to these facilities.
V.	RULINGS REQUESTED ON APPLICANTS' PROPOSED FINDINGS
Applicants propose findings and a conclusion at pages 12 through 15 of their brief. Under Tex. Gov't Code § 2001.141(e), Intervenor requests the following rulings. Accepting the uncontested history leaves the contested findings easier to see. On Applicants' proposed conclusion about PURA § 39.167, the Attorney General has filed an amicus brief in this docket observing that "[t]he Legislature directed the Commission to develop a plan, not to implement it in the manner it plans."

VI.	ADDITIONAL PROPOSED FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Intervenor proposes the following, in addition to proposed Findings R-1 through R-18 and Conclusions RCL-1 through RCL-3 in the Howton Remand Brief.
Proposed Findings of Fact
R-19.	For study year 2034, ERCOT's estimated consumer energy cost was $18.342 billion for the base case, $18.143 billion for the 345-kV plan, and $18.279 billion for the 765-kV plan. Applicants' Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 18-19.
R-20.	For study year 2039, ERCOT's estimated consumer energy cost was $22.070 billion for the base case, $22.143 billion for the 345-kV plan, and $21.914 billion for the 765-kV plan. Id.
R-21.	ERCOT estimated new construction cost at $30.75 billion for the 345-kV plan and $32.99 billion for the 765-kV plan. Applicants' Ex. 3 (Gurley Dir.), Ex. JG-4 at 7, Table E2.
R-22.	ERCOT's April 2026 Far West Import GTC exit strategy addressed a case in which approximately 2,500 MW of planned dispatchable generation in the Permian Basin materializes. Applicants' Ex. 14 (Martin Reb.) at 16-17, Ex. CMM-R-5 at 41-44.

Staff's witness agreed that the basis for need is the PBRP; that he had done no independent study of the need for the import paths at issue; that he had done no independent analysis or review of the costs of the import path; and that, assuming negative natural-gas prices at the Waha hub, it could potentially be more cost effective overall to ratepayers for LCRA or another legislatively created entity to own and operate dispatchable gas generation in the Path 2 area than to build Import Path 2. Tr. Vol. 3 at 262:8-21, 274:1-8, 275:4-11 (Poole Cross).

Tr. Vol. 4 at 59:17-60:3 (Cooley Cross).
R-26.	Staff's voltage analysis in Project No. 55718 was limited to issues unique to each voltage and did not analyze tariff exposure on steel and aluminum. Tr. Vol. 4 at 210:5-14 (Poole Cross).
Proposed Conclusions of Law
RCL-4.	Even if the proposed facilities are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard and are therefore exempt from clause (i), Applicants did not establish need under 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) and PURA § 37.056(c-1), for the reasons stated in Findings of Fact Nos. 87 through 148.
RCL-5.	Findings of fact adopted in Docket Nos. 59029, 59315, and 59336 are not evidence in this proceeding and, absent official notice, cannot substitute for findings based on this record. Tex. Gov't Code § 2001.141(c).
RCL-6.	PURA § 39.167 expired on September 1, 2025. It required development of a Permian Basin reliability plan; it did not itself grant a CCN or displace the certification requirements of PURA §§ 37.056-.057.
VII.	CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
The remand asks two questions. Applicants' answers rest on studies that assumed these facilities and on savings measured between two statewide plans. Their own filings say the PBRP was not intended to show TPL-001-5.1 compliance, the RTPs assumed the line, and no study removed it. ERCOT's own table shows the 765-kV plan costing consumers more than the 345-kV plan in 2034.
Intervenor Jason A. Howton respectfully requests that the ALJs, in the supplemental proposal for decision: (1) find that the record does not establish that the Bell County East to Big Hill facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; (2) find that the record contains no estimate of the congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from those facilities; (3) adopt the rulings requested in Section V; (4) adopt Proposed Findings R-1 through R-26 and Proposed Conclusions RCL-1 through RCL-6, or otherwise state the specific record evidence on which each remanded finding rests; (5) reaffirm the recommendation that the Commission deny the applications; and (6) grant such other relief to which Intervenor may be entitled.
